## From Fixed Levels to L(n): Building an Extensible Taxonomy System

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/extensible-taxonomy-system-yaml-seeding.html

Replaced a rigid 2-level sector/occupation taxonomy with a dynamic L(n) extensible system supporting arbitrary depth. Core is a flat adjacency list of TaxonomyNode objects stored in GCS, reconstructed into trees by pure functions. Zod validates structural integrity (no orphans, no cycles, consistent level labels). Ships with 4-level default (Sector > Sub Vertical > Function > Role) seeded from bundled YAML with version-gated deployment that prevents overwriting admin edits. GCS storage with CAS (conditional generation) writes for concurrent admin safety. Full admin CRUD UI (1,117 lines) with audit history. Bidirectional compat layer maps legacy sector/occupation to new taxonomy map — all existing API consumers work without changes. Cascading UI controls with dynamic filtering and multi-select chips. Agent prompts enriched with full taxonomy context. 7,026 lines, 61 files, 45 commits, 50 tests.

---

## When RAG Says Duplicate but the LLM Disagrees: Building an Adjudication Layer

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/llm-adjudication-dedup-false-positives.html

Added LLM second-opinion layer to RAG dedup gate to fix false-positive duplicates where tasks share persona/type but differ in subdomain context. Two-threshold band: below 0.75 auto-clears, 0.75-0.80 requires LLM review, above 0.80 RAG says duplicate but LLM gets override opportunity. LLM adjudicator submits candidate + top-K matches to auto-rater service (POST /api/v1/review with custom_evaluation_prompt), polls for structured judgment (isDuplicate, reason, confidence, durationMs). Fail-closed safety: LLM unavailability treats task as duplicate. Feature-flagged with 4 env vars, K8s configmap per environment. Runs in async Cloud Tasks workers, not user request path. 1,309 lines, 109 tests across 6 files.

---

## Building an Events Table for Pipeline Observability

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/events-table-pipeline-observability.html

Built a unified events table for a multi-step pipeline platform, aggregating events from four different sources into one diagnostic timeline. Events come from GCS manifest statusHistory (status transitions with actor/reason metadata), manifest actionHistory (admin actions like pause/cancel/reject), step trace files (execution data with QC results, dedup verdicts, agent metrics, error details), and database assignment lifecycle (created/claimed/closed). Instrumented 30 call sites across user routes, workers, batch services, and rework flows to record statusHistory transitions inside GCS CAS windows. Built causal event ordering with EVENT_TYPE_PRIORITY map for deterministic same-timestamp sort. Rich UI with context-specific error previews, QC breakdown panels, dedup detail panels, and client-side pagination after consolidation. Parallelized GCS reads from 13 serial round-trips to 3 parallel stages. 7,326 lines, 73 files, 64 commits.

## Dead Letter Queues for Pipeline Reliability

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/dead-letter-queue-pipeline-reliability.html

Implementing DLQ escalation for a multi-step pipeline engine. Two detection paths: inline (worker catches retries exhausted) and sweep (cron job detects stuck/orphaned runs past configurable thresholds). A dead letter registry defines reason codes (RETRIES_EXHAUSTED, STUCK_IN_PROGRESS, UNRECOVERED_ERROR) with env-overridable thresholds. DeadLetterService writes deadLettered/deadLetteredAt/deadLetterReason to GCS manifests and emits analytics events. Dead-lettered runs show red skull badges in the UI with a dedicated overlay in the status registry. Runs can be filtered via API parameter. Design philosophy: dead-lettering is a permanent, explicit signal that acknowledges the problem is unfixable at the system level and escalates to a human. The run stays visible but is clearly terminal.

---

## When Two Cache Layers Serve Stale Data

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/two-cache-layers-stale-data.html

Completed tasks showed stale "In Progress" state when reopened. Two independent cache layers both served old data. Root cause 1: Next.js unstable_cache on the detail API route had a 15s TTL, but the worker pipeline never called revalidateTag during step progression — adding it would create tight coupling, so the fix was removing the server cache entirely. Root cause 2: React Query's default gcTime of 5 minutes cached the response from the user's first visit; navigating away and back served the stale cached response before fetching fresh data. Fix: gcTime: 0 so cached data is discarded on navigation. Both fixes were needed — removing only one layer still served stale data from the other. The listing page worked correctly because it used a different data path, making the bug harder to diagnose.

---

## A UX Polish Sprint: 8 PRs in 48 Hours

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/ux-polish-sprint-filter-registry-consolidated-controls.html

Eight focused PRs shipped in 48 hours to polish an admin dashboard. (1) LISTING_FILTER_REGISTRY replacing hardcoded arrays — each filter entry declares key, label, icon, color, and matches() predicate; added Completed and virtual Duplicate filters. (2) MIN_SEARCH_QUERY_LENGTH = 3 with inline hint. (3) Consolidated 5 inline filter dropdowns into a single Filters DropdownMenu with active-count badge; toolbar went from 8 dense controls to [Filters (N)] [Sort] [Order] [Clear]. (4) Conditional task state filter that auto-hides when no paused/cancelled tasks exist. (5) Back button for batch detail. (6) Replaced internal jargon "Open A1" with "Assign Trainer". (7) Removed redundant arrow column. (8) Stale cache fix. No single PR is impressive; the compounding transforms the experience.

## GCS Race Conditions and Generation-Fenced Leases

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/gcs-race-conditions-generation-fenced-leases.html

Two race conditions in a distributed step-leasing system where stale workers could delete fresh locks. Race 1 (release path): Worker A's lease expires, Worker B acquires a fresh lease, Worker A finishes and calls release — the read-then-delete was non-atomic, so the token check passed against stale data and the delete removed Worker B's valid lease. Race 2 (reclaim path): when acquiring a lease over an expired one, the unconditional delete could remove another worker's freshly acquired lease between the read and delete. Fix: GCS generation-based fencing. Every lease read captures the GCS object generation number. Every delete passes `ifGenerationMatch`. If another worker overwrote the lease, GCS returns 412 Precondition Failed and the delete is a no-op. Same principle as database row versioning or HTTP ETags — optimistic concurrency control applied to cloud object storage with zero additional infrastructure.

---

## Multi-Layer Caching for Dashboard Latency

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/multi-layer-cache-dashboard-latency.html

Four-layer caching strategy to reduce an admin dashboard from multi-second loads to sub-second. Layer 1: HTTP Cache-Control headers matched to data volatility — taxonomy data at 1h public cache, pool availability at 5s private, run listings with short TTL. Layer 2: Next.js unstable_cache wrapping GCS fan-out with 30s TTL and tag-based invalidation — every mutation calls revalidateTag to bust the cache. Layer 3: React Query migration with staleTime: Infinity for stable data, parallel queries via useQueries, and a centralized hierarchical query key registry (autoSeedKeys) for type-safe invalidation cascading. Layer 4: dynamic imports for 8 step viewers reducing initial JS bundle. Plus: useAutoSeedUrlState hook storing tab/batch/filters/sort in URL search params for shareable dashboard state, and batch drill-down optimization filtering from already-loaded task lists instead of new GCS round-trips.

## Pipeline Hardening: Timeouts, Traceability, and Graceful Shutdown

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/pipeline-hardening-timeouts-traceability-graceful-shutdown.html

Three production issues in a pipeline engine. Problem 1: uniform 1800s dispatch deadline meant 10-minute steps held queue slots for 30 minutes. Fix: dispatch registry — frozen array + Map index defining per-step agent timeout, dispatch deadline, and env var override keys. Problem 2: Cloud Tasks dispatch deadline kills left tasks stuck in_progress with no error — silent container termination. Fix: SIGTERM handler with in-flight lease registry that releases all held leases and writes trace events before exit. Also fixed Zod validation errors being swallowed (only err.message logged, not err.code/err.details) and QC gate failures missing remediation text. Problem 3: static 1-hour lease TTL regardless of step duration. Fix: dynamic TTL derived from dispatch deadline + 5-minute buffer. Plus three long-horizon handoff fixes: skip manifest reset on duplicate replays, gate author-slot opening on fully successful output, reapply task.toml rewrite on crash recovery.

## Building a GCS-Backed Auto-Seeder Platform

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/gcs-backed-auto-seeder-platform.html

Replacing a desktop tool with a web-based task seeding platform while avoiding throwaway code. Humza Tareen built a three-layer provider-service-route architecture where services depend on a provider interface, not a concrete storage backend. The GcsProvider stores run metadata as .manifest.json files in GCS. When Prisma is ready, a PrismaProvider implements the same interface with zero changes to services or routes. A client-side V1 adapter transforms between GCS API types and frontend types, isolating the UI from backend changes. An artifact kind registry infers file types from extension, MIME, and path patterns. A step registry handles step ID disambiguation. The pipeline was expanded from 11 flat steps to 13 nodes (10 steps + 3 gates) with a centralized status registry as single source of truth for all status definitions, labels, icons, colors, and sort order. The task detail page was unified to a single API call (from 3 parallel fetches), with model output and golden data viewers matching desktop terminology for zero user retraining.

## When 57K Lines Get Rolled Back

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/57k-line-merge-rollback-reconsolidation.html

A 57,000-line auto-seeder feature across 334 files was split into 11 stacked PRs (schema, Zod schemas, DB layer, API routes, agent engine, pipeline steps, services, lib layer, UI, dashboard, K8s infrastructure). Each got reviewed independently (2-4 approvals). But cross-dependencies meant individual PRs couldn't merge cleanly — test failures cascaded. All 11 merged into an integration branch and shipped as a single squashed commit. The next day it was rolled back — too large to confidently debug in production. The reconsolidation used the rollback as an opportunity: merged two overlapping directories (auto-seed/ and auto-seeder/) into a single src/lib/v1/ with strict provider → service → route layering. A single GcsRepository class became the only GCS touchpoint. Pure domain logic separated into domain/. Business logic into services/. Worker engine into pipeline/. Net result: -9,685 lines from the original. Database migrations were split to a separate PR. Lesson: split PRs are great for review but terrible for integration with cross-dependencies; the rollback forced a better architecture than the original.

## Invisible Bugs: File Type Bypass and Missing Worker Runs

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/invisible-bugs-file-type-bypass-missing-worker-runs.html

Two production bugs invisible during development. Bug 1: Expert review file uploads validated against a global extension allowlist (.docx, .xlsx, .pdf), but a reviewer could upload a .pdf to replace a .docx — the allowlist accepted PDFs even though the downstream pipeline expected matching types. Fixed with two-layer validation: server-side validateFileTypeMatch() rejects extension mismatches, client-side dropzone restricts accept to the original file's extension. 10 unit tests. Bug 2: Admin bulk-approve changed task status to COMPLETED but never created the EXPERT_QUALITY_CHECK worker run record. The Delivery Completed tab query requires both the stage and the worker run. Normal expert review creates it automatically; the admin bypass skipped it. Fixed with upsert (empty update to avoid overwriting existing runs), non-blocking so status changes succeed even if worker run creation fails. 11 new test cases, 83 total. Both bugs share a root cause: bypass paths that skip steps the normal flow performs automatically.

## Designing a Task Lifecycle V1 from Scratch

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/task-lifecycle-v1-schema-api-design.html

The existing system tracked tasks with a flat status column and scattered metadata — no version history, no step tracking, no structured audit trail. Humza Tareen designed and implemented a complete task lifecycle system: 10 Prisma tables with composite keys and immutable versioning. TaskV1 with status derived from a currentStepId FK pointer (no separate status column). TaskVersionV1 as immutable snapshots updated first in transactions. StepV1 with a 13-status state machine. Separate event tables for task pipeline (linear) and eval pipeline (parallel trials) to prevent cross-contamination. PromptV1 and DataV1 with model/agent/provider as dedicated columns for search. EvalV1/TrialV1 with composite unique constraints. Transactional write order: insert event, update version pointer, update task pointer — all in one Prisma transaction. The API layer was delivered in 6 stacked PRs: pipeline infrastructure with registries (119 tests), tasks/versions CRUD (7 routes, 19 tests), steps/events with transition validation returning 409 on invalid moves (6 routes, 14 tests), prompts/data CRUD (4 routes, 9 tests), evals/trials/insights (10 routes, 15 tests), and auto-seed API with GCS stubs. Total: 40+ routes, 176+ tests.

End-to-end SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) recording pipeline for capturing human demonstration data. Docker-based desktop environments with VNC access, auto-retry on container failures, lifecycle management, optional snapshot before termination. Rubric-based review with approve/reject/changes-requested outcomes, rework flow with reviewer feedback, worker notifications via Firestore and FCM. 12 admin pages: worker queue, task detail with embedded VNC sandbox viewer, sandbox management, review queue, bulk CSV import, stats dashboards. ## When Display Labels Break Sorting

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/unified-status-sort-display-labels.html

The admin submissions page had a Status column that looked correct but sorted wrong. Three interacting bugs: (1) computeUnifiedRank took (stage, status, failureReason) but the same database stage/status mapped to different display labels depending on review results and worker runs — PRE_QA:ACTIVE could be "Checking Quality", "Quality Check Failed", or "Quality Check Passed", all with the same rank. Fixed by adding reviewPassed and workerRuns parameters, assigning unique ranks 0-13 for all 14 pipeline statuses. (2) Tiebreaker within same rank was CUID string comparison with no date correlation — rows appeared in random order within a status group. Fixed with date (newest first) as secondary key plus task ID as stable tiebreaker. (3) The 5,000-row window query had no orderBy clause, returning arbitrary rows when total exceeded the cap. Fixed with deterministic ordering. The Prisma select had to expand to include reviews and workerRuns for accurate rank computation. 78 new tests covering rank splits, backward compatibility, uniqueness, sort direction, date sub-sort, and null handling.

## Taming a State Machine: Bulk Admin Ops

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/enterprise-state-machine-bulk-admin-ops.html

The initial bulk status change API was clean in theory — atomic transactions, event sourcing, preview mode. Then it hit real users and QA. The state machine had 13+ source statuses with different valid transition targets. Humza Tareen spent 13 commits over 4 days hardening it: building a transition rule matrix (13x6 grid) to prevent invalid admin moves, fixing a subtle where-clause bug in "Quality Check Failed" that matched any failed review even when a later review passed, decoupling workflow dispatch to default-OFF so admins don't accidentally trigger expensive pipelines, fixing unified status resolution bugs where output generation and expert quality check worker types were filtered out of the query (extracted STATUS_RELEVANT_WORKER_TYPES as a shared constant), adding JSON file upload with persistent row selection across filter/sort/pagination changes, capping unified sort at 5,000 rows with a truncation header, and adding an isTerminalStatus() guard to prevent analytics inflation from non-terminal status changes.

## Decoupling Claim Timeouts from Feature Flags

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/claim-timeout-decoupling-expert-review-ux.html

The expert review pool had a feature toggle. Disabling it to stop new claims also killed the countdown timer for already-claimed tasks, giving reviewers infinite time. Humza Tareen decoupled the timeout configuration from the pool toggle so admins can set claim timeouts even when the pool is disabled. The cron job releasing stale claims was gated by expertPoolEnabled — widened to also fire when expert review is active. Redesigned the countdown into three phases: normal display, urgent amber warning below 15 minutes, and expired red state with pulsing animation. After expiry, upload and submit buttons are disabled with contextual reason text. A hidden 5-minute grace period in the cron job was documented in admin UI hints. New tests cover pool enabled + timeout, pool disabled + timeout, expired claims with pending uploads, and the grace period boundary.

## Production-Ready Multi-Turn Evaluation

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/production-ready-multi-turn-evaluation.html

The basic multi-turn runner worked but wasn't production-ready. Humza Tareen hardened it with per-turn harness evaluation (invoking the test suite against the agent's patch inside Docker after each turn to determine if a fix is valid, not just that a patch exists), codebase snapshots (capturing tar.gz via base64 transfer from Docker containers for post-hoc debugging), artifact validation with retry (checking .traj, .patch, and snapshot files exist and are non-empty, retrying on transient Docker failures), resume state management (tracking completed tasks in .resume_state.json for crash recovery without re-running everything), completeness reports (per-task/per-turn completion stats and error details), and resolution summaries (identifying the first turn where a test started passing). Each turn writes incremental JSONL files matching the deliverable structure expected by downstream tools.

## Audit-Safe Admin Tools with Event Sourcing

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/audit-safe-admin-bulk-operations.html

The delivery team needed to change task statuses in bulk, but this required engineers to run ad-hoc SQL scripts against production — no audit trail, no validation, no rollback context. Humza Tareen built a single API endpoint with preview and execute modes: preview validates all inputs and shows what would happen; execute performs the changes. Each task update is wrapped in a Prisma $transaction — status update and event creation happen atomically. Event sourcing creates task_events records with source, previous/new state, actor identity from Firebase auth, reason text, and merged metadata from previous events. The endpoint is wrapped with withAudit middleware requiring Firebase admin claims. Input validation caps batches at 50 tasks, enum-checks statuses, and limits reason text to 4096 characters. A slide-over UI component provides status selection, live preview, and persistent row selection across data refreshes.

## I Built a Starter Repo That Turns AI Coding Tools Into Senior Engineers

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/dev-starter-kit-ai-coding-tools.html

Every new project starts the same way: no CI, no linting, no test enforcement, no issue templates. Humza Tareen extracted development practices from multiple production projects — a multi-cluster AI evaluation platform on GCP and Python evaluation pipelines — into a single, clone-and-go open-source starter repo.

The repo includes: three GitHub Actions workflows (PR checks with Ruff auto-fix and commit-back, test coverage enforcement that posts PR comments with exact test file/class/method names, incremental linting, merge readiness gates), pre-commit hooks (Ruff, syntax checks, YAML/JSON/TOML validation, private key detection, branch protection), structured issue templates (bug reports, incident reports, infrastructure issues), and an incident runbook with severity classification, triage checklists, and diagnostic commands.

The differentiator: instruction files for every major AI coding tool — AGENTS.md (Codex, Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf), CLAUDE.md (Claude Code sessions), .cursor/rules/*.mdc (modular glob-scoped Cursor rules), .claude/rules/*.md (Claude Code scoped rules), and .github/copilot-instructions.md (GitHub Copilot). These files teach AI tools to follow the same development loop a senior engineer would: read before editing, lint after every change, test after every change, write tests for new code, use conventional commits, never commit secrets.

Key design decisions: structural test coverage enforcement (did you change test files alongside source files?) over coverage percentage, auto-fix in CI to eliminate formatting follow-up commits, multiple AI tool formats for maximum compatibility, pre-commit AND CI for defense in depth.

Repo: https://github.com/humzakt/dev-starter-kit — MIT licensed.

## Building an AI Evaluation Platform on GCP: Architecture of a Multi-Cluster System

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/building-ai-evaluation-platform-gcp.html

How do you evaluate whether an AI coding agent is actually good at writing code? Over the past 6 months, Humza Tareen built a production AI evaluation platform on GCP. The architecture includes multiple Cloud Run services with auto-scaling (0-100 instances per service), multiple GKE clusters (up to 39 nodes, n2-standard-8 + n2-highmem-4), Cloud SQL PostgreSQL instances with Regional HA, dozens of Pub/Sub topics with dead-letter queues, multiple Firestore databases, GCS storage buckets, and Cloud Tasks for reliable async execution.

Key services: Evaluation Engine (task lifecycle management), Auto-Rating Service (LLM output scoring via LiteLLM proxy), RAG Retrieval Service (pgvector similarity search), RL Training Arena (Gym-style reinforcement learning), Guard Service (Google OIDC, JWT, API keys), Notification Service (Cloud Tasks with exponential backoff), Workflow Orchestration (WebSocket HITL workflows).

Key decision: Cloud Run for stateless request-response (scales to zero, bills per-request), GKE for stateful long-running workloads (persistent connections, GPU access). Both AlloyDB and Firestore used — AlloyDB for ACID transactions and complex JOINs, Firestore for real-time state and sub-second writes.

Numbers: High merge rate, continuous deployment, hundreds of issues filed and resolved across severity levels.

Tech stack: Python (FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic), TypeScript (React), GCP (Cloud Run, GKE, Cloud Tasks, Pub/Sub, AlloyDB, Firestore, Cloud Build, GCS, Cloud Scheduler, Secret Manager, Cloud Monitoring), PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker, GitHub Actions.

## Event-Driven Architecture on GCP: Pub/Sub, Cloud Tasks, and Cloud Scheduler

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/event-driven-architecture-gcp-pubsub.html

I learned the hard way that synchronous HTTP calls don't work when your pipeline takes 30 minutes and touches 6 different services. Timeouts, retry nightmares, and cascading failures — I'd been there. That's when I rebuilt everything around events, and it changed how I think about distributed systems. Each service now subscribes independently, retries from its own checkpoint, and doesn't care if another service is down. The pipeline flows through six phases: Task Creation → Preprocessing → Agent Execution → Output Collection → Judging & Scoring → Aggregation & Learning, all orchestrated via Pub/Sub topics. I discovered patterns that saved me countless hours: fan-out subscriptions that let me add new consumers without touching publishers, dead-letter queues that caught 6 production issues before they became outages, and Cloud Scheduler automating everything. But the real win was learning when to use Pub/Sub (events) versus Cloud Tasks (commands), and why acknowledging after commit — not before — prevents data loss. Here's how event-driven architecture transformed a fragile system into something that actually works in production.

## Debugging AlloyDB SSL Connection Drops

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/debugging-alloydb-ssl-connection-drops.html

For two weeks, 5% of our evaluation tasks were failing with cryptic SSL errors. No pattern, no logs, just random failures that made debugging feel impossible. I checked connection pools, retry logic, network timeouts — nothing made sense. Then I discovered the culprit: AlloyDB was silently dropping idle SSL connections after 10 minutes, but SQLAlchemy's connection pool was configured to recycle after 15 minutes. Dead connections were being handed out to new requests, and they'd fail the moment they tried to execute a query. The fix was just 3 lines — setting pool_recycle to 180 seconds and enabling pool_pre_ping — but finding it took two weeks of detective work. Combined with idempotent writes for Cloud Tasks retry safety, we went from a 5% failure rate to 0.01%. This is the story of how a silent connection drop turned into a production incident, and what I learned about debugging distributed systems when nothing makes sense.

---

## Idempotent Cloud Tasks Handlers in Python

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/idempotent-cloud-tasks-handlers-python.html

Cloud Tasks promises at-least-once delivery, which sounds great until you realize "at least once" means "maybe twice, or three times, or more." I learned this the hard way when duplicate records started appearing in our database — same task, executed multiple times, creating the same data over and over. That's when I built a simple 3-step pattern that made Cloud Tasks retries safe: generate deterministic IDs from payloads using SHA-256 hashing, use PostgreSQL's INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING to silently ignore duplicates, and always return HTTP 200 (returning 409 causes infinite retry loops). I also learned to cap Cloud Run's containerConcurrency to 10-20 instead of the default 80, preventing database connection exhaustion under load. This pattern now handles thousands of tasks per day with zero duplicates, and it's saved me from countless production bugs. Here's how to make Cloud Tasks idempotent, and why it matters more than you think.

## Zero-Downtime Embedding Migration in Production RAG System

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/rag-embedding-migration-zero-downtime.html

The email came on a Friday afternoon: our embedding model was being deprecated in 48 hours. No warning, no migration path, just "you have two days to replace everything." Our RAG system depended on those embeddings for every search query, and we had millions of vectors stored in pgvector. I couldn't take the system down — production workloads were running 24/7. So I built a migration plan that would let us switch models without a single second of downtime: make the model configurable via environment variables, add new vector columns alongside the old ones (never replace — ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY), run batch re-embedding with progress tracking, flip a feature flag to switch traffic, and validate by comparing search results (82% average overlap between old and new). Forty-eight hours later, we'd migrated everything with zero downtime and zero data loss. This is how I learned that the best migrations are the ones users never notice.

## RL Training Arena for AI Code Agents

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/rl-training-arena-code-agents.html

I wanted to train AI coding agents using reinforcement learning, but I needed a safe way to execute untrusted code at scale. That's how I ended up building a Gym-style RL environment on GKE, where agents learn to write code by actually running it — and failing safely. The Executor Service creates episodes, executes steps, and computes rewards, but the real challenge was sandboxing: how do you run arbitrary code from AI agents without compromising your infrastructure? Cloud Build became the answer — it gave me isolated, ephemeral execution environments that could scale to hundreds of concurrent episodes. I built Redis-based episode state management, Firestore trajectory logging, and a Preprocessor Service that generates dynamic verifiers and analyzes repositories. Using hexagonal architecture made everything portable, and multiple GKE auto-scaling clusters handle the load. This is how I learned that training AI agents requires infrastructure that can fail safely, and why Cloud Build's sandboxing was the key to making it work.

## Security Audit: Critical Security Gaps Found

URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/security-audit-ai-platform-25-critical-issues.html

I decided to audit my own production platform, thinking I'd find a few minor issues. Instead, I discovered 25 critical security vulnerabilities that could have compromised everything. SQL injection through BigQuery f-strings, hardcoded credentials in alembic.ini, secrets leaking in CI/CD logs, missing authentication on internal endpoints, PII stored in plaintext logs — the list went on. But the architecture issues were just as bad: a monolithic God Class that violated every principle of clean code, V1/V2 dependency leakage causing unpredictable behavior, in-memory rate limiting that didn't work across Cloud Run instances, and CPU-bound algorithms blocking the async event loop. I spent weeks fixing everything: moving all secrets to GCP Secret Manager, switching to parameterized queries, implementing structured logging with PII stripping, adding authentication middleware to every endpoint, and setting up pre-commit hooks for security scanning. I broke the God Class into 5 focused services, built an LLM Gateway abstraction, moved rate limiting to Redis, and filed hundreds of GitHub issues to track it all. This is what happens when you audit your own code — and why it's the most important thing you can do.

### Article 16: Incident Response & CLI Agent Debugging
URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/incident-response-iflow-debugging.html
Published: 2026-02-12

When you're running an AI evaluation platform that orchestrates agent execution across GKE clusters, "something broke" isn't useful. This week I built incident response infrastructure — a runbook with 70+ diagnostic commands — and debugged a chain of silent failures. CLI tools that exit code 0 on API errors. Shallow git clones breaking PR diff analysis. Case-sensitive agent keys in PostgreSQL causing config changes to silently target the wrong row. Each fix was small; diagnosing each required tracing through three layers. The lesson: invest in observability before you need it.

---

### Article 17: Systematic Service Hardening
URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/systematic-service-hardening-guard-notification.html
Published: 2026-02-12

One week, three production services, zero downtime. I hardened the auth gateway (N+1 queries turning 50-team listings into 100+ DB calls, non-atomic counter increments losing data, SSRF via route URL injection, tokens in localStorage), the notification service (race conditions in 4 subsystems, in-memory-only DLQ, fire-and-forget event publishing), and the auto-rater (no mathematical correctness tests for scoring algorithms, missing database indexes). Plus 124 unit tests where there were zero, Trivy scanning, rate limiting, and enum validation at the database level. Not glamorous, but production systems that don't get hardened become production incidents.

---

### Article 18: How I Find Bugs in Production Code
URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/production-bug-hunting-33-issues.html
Published: 2026-02-12

I filed 33 issues in one week across four production services using a 5-layer audit methodology. Layer 1 (API Surface): limit=-1 returning entire datasets. Layer 2 (Auth): any authenticated user reading any other user's tasks. Layer 3 (Data Integrity): same PR URL creating unlimited concurrent tasks. Layer 4 (Error Handling): analytics loading unbounded result sets. Layer 5 (Security): path traversal in file content endpoints, CORS reflecting any origin with credentials, 128 API paths exposed publicly. The bugs that surprised me: 145 uses of deprecated datetime.utcnow(), OpenAPI docs exposing internal endpoints, webhook secrets not enforced in dev. 11 of 33 issues closed within 3 days.

---

How I built test coverage enforcement, dynamic test discovery, and CI gates that actually catch bugs before they reach production. The gates caught invisible test files that weren't being run and prevented broken code from shipping. Covers GitHub Actions, Python, FastAPI, and practical patterns for making CI/CD quality gates effective rather than ceremonial.

A logging adapter collision was crashing agent sessions in production. Here's how I built crash-proof logging infrastructure with safe_log_extra helpers and structured error recovery. The lesson: your observability stack can become a single point of failure if it isn't designed to fail gracefully.

### Multi-Turn Agent Evaluation at Scale
URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/multi-turn-agent-evaluation-persistent-state.html
Published: 2026-03-13
Tags: AI Agents, Docker, Python, Evaluation, Multi-Turn
Summary: Single-turn AI agent evaluation runs each attempt independently — no conversation memory, fresh Docker containers, hints concatenated into growing prompts. The result: zero successful patches. This post covers building a multi-turn runner that maintains persistent Docker environments, preserves conversation history and code edits across turns, and injects progressive hints naturally. It also covers the config discovery where a call limit of 60 caused 100% budget exhaustion, and how raising it to 300 (validated in production) produced successful patches across multiple programming languages.

### Docker Image Hardening for AI Benchmarks
URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/docker-image-hardening-ai-benchmarks.html
Published: 2026-03-13
Tags: Docker, Infrastructure, Python, CI/CD, AI Benchmarks
Summary: Multi-language AI coding benchmarks use Docker images with repo snapshots for each task. Many images lack Python, have broken git repos, or missing dependencies — causing agents to explore indefinitely and exhaust budgets. This post covers injecting miniconda + agent runtime layers into arbitrary language images, pre-flight validation that checks Docker images before expensive evaluations run, skip lists for known-broken images, and completion detection to avoid repeating work on reruns.

### Adding Responses API Support to an Agent Framework
URL: https://humzakt.github.io/blog/responses-api-support-agent-framework.html
Published: 2026-03-13
Tags: OpenAI, Responses API, Python, LLM, Agent Framework
Summary: When codex-family models required the Responses API instead of Chat Completions, the agent framework needed a new code path. This post covers auto-detecting which API to use, converting Chat Completions messages (system → developer role, content blocks), flattening nested tool schemas to the Responses API format, and normalizing polymorphic response output back to the standard format. All without touching the existing Chat Completions path — validated by 64 unit tests.
